scope: Industry and consumer facts for Australians booking destination wedding travel (ATIA, ACCC, Smartraveller, state consumer regulators, hotel group block terms)
method_note: FAST mode, one round. ACCC travel page and Smartraveller insurance page were fetched and read in full (confidence high). ATIA pages returned 404 or a bot check on direct fetch, so ATIA facts rest on ATIA page text returned by search (confidence medium); verify live before publishing. No competitor or agency blog used as a source.

facts.claim: Australian Consumer Law consumer guarantees apply to travel services whether the consumer books directly with the airline, cruise line or tour operator, through a travel agent, or through a third party such as a booking platform or travel package provider.

These consumer guarantees cover travel services within Australia, travel services by international businesses departing Australia, and travel to Australia from another country booked through a provider's Australian website.
facts.use_note: Outbound travel from Australia is covered; legs wholly overseas booked with a foreign supplier are not stated as covered. Do not overstate.

facts.claim: If a delayed or cancelled travel service is not replaced within a reasonable time, the provider must give the consumer their choice of a different replacement service or a refund.
There is no single definition of a 'reasonable time'; the ACCC does not decide it (a court or tribunal does), and factors such as the purpose of the consumer's travel may be relevant.

Providers do not have to give a replacement or refund under the consumer guarantees if the consumer changes their mind or misses the service for unrelated reasons, or if a third party (for example a government restriction) prevents the service; rights then depend on the booking's terms and conditions.

When booking through a travel agent or intermediary, both the agent's and the primary provider's terms and conditions apply, and agents are usually bound by the primary provider's terms; legally they may only need to pass on the remedy the primary provider offers.
facts.use_note: Key honest point for the article: an advisor does not add legal rights beyond the supplier's; the value is in reading and negotiating terms.

facts.claim: ACCC tips when arriving on time is critical: consider a fare class with better options if there is a delay or cancellation, allow extra time between connections, check the agent's and supplier's terms (including any force majeure term) before booking, and ask for unclear terms to be confirmed in writing.

The ACCC does not resolve individual complaints about delayed or cancelled travel; the first step is to contact the travel service provider, then take the problem further (state or territory consumer agencies, tribunals) if unresolved.

If a business you prepaid or paid a deposit to becomes insolvent, you may become an unsecured creditor; ACCC suggests checking whether the administrator will honour the transaction, registering as a creditor, or asking your bank or card provider about a chargeback, and notes compensation funds exist only for some industries in some states.
facts.use_note: Taken from ACCC page text returned by search, not a full fetch. Re-read the page before quoting.

facts.claim: ATIA (Australian Travel Industry Association) retired the ATAS accreditation designator on 25 October 2024; eligible businesses are now designated 'ATIA Accredited'.
facts.use_note: ATIA site restructured; this URL returned 404 on direct fetch. Text came from ATIA pages via search. Verify on atia.travel before linking.

facts.claim: ATIA Accredited businesses must comply with a Code of Conduct that includes a service quality promise, appropriately trained staff and full transparency of terms and conditions before booking; applicants also undergo a National Police check.
facts.use_note: Search-returned ATIA text; not fetched directly.

facts.claim: ATIA states accreditation is a point-in-time assessment, is voluntary, is not a government body, and is not a guarantee of solvency nor an insurance or compensation scheme.
facts.use_note: Important caveat: do not imply accreditation protects money if an agent collapses.

facts.claim: Travellers can check whether an agent or tour operator is currently ATIA Accredited by searching ATIA's TravelTick consumer directory (traveltick.com.au), which is also where complaints to ATIA are lodged.
facts.use_note: Page sits behind a bot check; text from search. Confirm traveltick.com.au is live before linking.

facts.claim: ATIA publishes a list of cancelled and withdrawn accreditations.

Smartraveller says the right travel insurance is as essential as a passport for overseas travel, and Australians should get insurance regardless of who they are, where they are going and what they are doing.
Always read the Product Disclosure Statement (PDS) before buying; it sets out inclusions, exclusions, definitions, the claims process and emergency support.

Choose a policy covering every country on the trip including stopovers and transit points, make sure the destination is not at 'Do not travel', and check whether the policy covers cancellation if the advice level rises after booking.

Insurers exclude many activities from standard policies (even common ones such as cruises), so travellers may need to pay extra or buy a specialised policy and should check the included and excluded activities list.
Travellers must tell their insurer about all pre-existing health conditions; most policies have an age limit and mature Australians often pay more for cover.
facts.use_note: Relevant to the paying_parent persona and older guests.

facts.claim: Policies often limit each valuable item's value; adding cover for valuables can range from hundreds to thousands of dollars, and travellers should check item limits and the excess.
facts.use_note: Relevant to rings, gowns and suits travelling overseas. Not a price claim, no Nic sign-off needed.

facts.claim: Free credit card travel insurance often covers fewer situations with lower item limits than comprehensive policies, and usually has to be activated; do not assume it is.
Travel insurance can cover cancellation costs if plans change; basic medical-only policies usually do not cover cancellation costs or property.
Travellers usually are not covered if something goes wrong while under the influence of alcohol or drugs; even a low blood alcohol level can get a claim denied.
facts.use_note: Useful, tactful guest-briefing point for wedding celebrations.

facts.claim: Medical assistance is usually the highest unexpected cost for Australians overseas, and the Australian Government cannot pay travellers' bills; it expects all Australians to take out appropriate insurance.

Under a transition plan approved in December 2012, the Travel Compensation Fund and state travel agent licensing were removed from 1 July 2014, with consumers relying instead on Australian Consumer Law protections and credit card chargebacks.
facts.use_note: Search-returned text, not fetched. Queensland trust deed suggests the fund's final wind-up ran to 2015, so say licensing and the fund 'were phased out from mid-2014' rather than a single close date.

facts.claim: Hotel group room blocks use a cut-off date after which unreserved rooms return to general sale, and attrition clauses that charge the group if pickup falls below the agreed commitment; published examples include a Marriott property's group terms (14-day cut-off) and IHG property wedding-block policies (30-day cut-off).
facts.use_note: Property-level documents (one EMEA Marriott, one US IHG), not group-wide policy, and terms are negotiable. Only use to explain the concepts of cut-off and attrition generically; do not quote the day counts as standard.
